macro.basis: provisional, H1 2026 (GSS); IMF projects 5.7% for full-year 2026 (p.24)
macro.comment: Growth comfortably beat the 4.8% floor in the first half, and the full-year projection of 5.7% is also above target.
Non-oil growth of 5.9% in the first half beat the 4.9% target.

macro.basis: latest month reported (October 2026); December outturn not yet available
macro.comment: Inflation ran below the 6-10% band (it fell to 3.2% in March), so the target was undershot rather than hit; the budget calls 5.5% 'within the end-year target band' although it is under the band floor.
The budget projects a full-year primary surplus of 1.6% of GDP (GH¢26.2bn) after 1.4% by October, meeting the 1.5% fiscal-rule target on current projections.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); provisional Jan-Oct -1.0% per text (p.61), -1.3% in Appendix 2A
macro.comment: The projected deficit of 2.0% of GDP is smaller than the 2.2% target; the budget's Jan-Oct comparison uses a mid-year programme of -3.0%.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); provisional Jan-Oct -2.3% vs programme -4.5% (p.66)
macro.comment: The projected cash deficit of 3.8% of GDP is slightly better than the 4.0% target.
The cash primary balance is projected at -0.2% of GDP, better than the -0.4% target.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); provisional Jan-Oct GH¢219.3bn, 3.5% above programme (p.62)
macro.comment: Revenue is projected to exceed the budget by about 2%, after running 3.5% ahead of target to October.
Domestic revenue is projected at 17.0% of GDP (GH¢271.5bn) against a 16.6% target.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); Jan-Oct tax revenue GH¢174.4bn was 1.2% below programme
macro.comment: Total tax revenue is projected marginally above budget, although non-oil tax and especially VAT ran below target to October (p.62, p.68).

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); Jan-Oct GH¢1.0bn vs GH¢2.1bn programme (p.63)
macro.comment: Grant inflows are projected about 21% below budget and were roughly half of target to October.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); Jan-Oct GH¢235.1bn was 9.3% below programme (p.63)
macro.comment: Spending was under programme to October, but the end-year projection exceeds the 2026 expenditure ceiling by about GH¢3.0bn (1%), driven by transfers to earmarked funds.

macro.basis: projected end-year (Appendix 2A); Jan-Oct GH¢41.4bn vs GH¢45.3bn programme (p.64)
macro.comment: Capex is projected about 11% below the original budget; the mid-year revision had already cut the allocation to GH¢52.5bn, and foreign-financed capex lagged.

macro.basis: provisional Jan-Oct vs Jan-Oct programme GH¢24.3bn; the end-year 'projection' in Appendix 2A simply restates the budget figure
macro.comment: About 70% of the annual amount was cleared by October, 14% behind the period programme; the budget says no new arrears were accumulated (p.55).
Reserves covered 4.5 months of imports, well above the 3-month floor (the budget gives both US$12.7bn (p.55) and US$12.1bn (p.82) for the same date).
Bad loans fell from 20.4% to 14.0% but remain well above the 10% end-2026 target, and the budget only expects further improvement in 2027 (p.89).
Higher oil prices pushed receipts 38% above the full-year projection within ten months.

macro.target_label: No 2026 debt target set (fiscal rule: below 45% of GDP by 2035)
macro.comment: There is no 2026 debt-ratio target to judge against; debt was 47.5% of GDP, below the ECOWAS 70% ceiling but above the 45% long-term anchor.
The 2026 budget set no exchange-rate target; the 10.1% depreciation narrowly missed the ECOWAS ±10% convergence criterion (p.25).

commitments.outcome: Real GDP grew 6.2% in the first half of 2026 against the 4.8% target; the IMF projects 5.7% for the full year (p.24).
Non-oil GDP grew 5.9% in the first half of 2026 against the 4.9% target.
Inflation was 5.5% in October 2026 after falling to 3.2% in March; this is below the 6-10% band, so the 8% target was undershot rather than hit.
The primary surplus (commitment) was 1.4% of GDP for Jan-Oct, described as on course for 1.5% (p.61); Appendix 2A projects 1.6% of GDP (GH¢26.2bn) for the full year.
The projected end-2026 overall deficit is 2.0% of GDP (commitment) and 3.8% (cash), both inside the 2.2% / 4.0% targets; Jan-Oct deficits were 1.0% and 2.3% (p.61).
Gross international reserves stood at 4.5 months of import cover at end-September 2026.
Revenue and grants are projected at GH¢274.0bn (17.2% of GDP) for 2026, above the GH¢268.1bn target; Jan-Oct receipts of GH¢219.3bn were 3.5% above programme (p.62).
Non-oil tax revenue was GH¢167.2bn in Jan-Oct, below the GH¢170.0bn programme, with VAT short because of non-compliance (p.68); no full-year non-oil tax figure is given.
The 2027 budget does not report a 2026 non-oil revenue-to-GDP figure to compare with the 15.7% target.
The VAT Act, 2025 (Act 1151) took effect at the start of 2026 with a reduced effective VAT rate and a GH¢750,000 registration threshold; the COVID-19 levy is not mentioned separately.

The Customs Act, 2026 (Act 1179) and Excise Act, 2026 (Act 1180) have been enacted, but the Income Tax Bill is still with the Attorney-General for drafting and is expected to be enacted in early 2027 (p.68, p.91).
Spending was 9.3% below programme to October (p.63), but Appendix 2A projects 2026 expenditure of GH¢305.5bn (19.1% of GDP), above the GH¢302.5bn ceiling.

GH¢20.8bn of arrears was cleared by October against a GH¢24.3bn period programme, and the budget states no new arrears were allowed (p.55); the full-year figure in Appendix 2A merely restates the budget.
The 2027 budget does not report 2026 payments to IPPs under the renegotiated agreements.
No award of ECG distribution concessions is reported; the budget now says private-sector participation in distribution will be fully implemented by end-2027.
The 2027 budget does not report on restoring the World Bank-backed standby letters of credit.
Not yet started: the plant has been enlarged to 1,450MW at Kafodzidzi-Abrobeano and construction is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with the first 600MW due by December 2028.
The rural electrification initiative is being implemented in Central, Oti, Savannah and Volta, with 601 communities in 47 districts earmarked for completion by year-end.
Only the conclusion of negotiations on Voltaian Basin exploration rights with GNPC, Explorco and Chrome Energy is reported; no drilling start is mentioned.
AKSA's Anwomaso plant (205MW, 175MW net) is complete and running, and CENIT's 100MW plant is synchronised to the grid with commissioning being finalised; AKSA is to expand to 350MW in 2027.
GH¢14.3bn was spent on the Big Push by October 2026 against the GH¢30bn allocation; no count of completed projects is given and the mid-2027 completion milestone is not yet due.
The 2027 budget does not report on the 10km-per-constituency road programme.
Routine maintenance covered 17,143km (2,996km trunk, 9,250km feeder, 4,897km urban) plus minor rehabilitation of 494km, short of the 25,000km target; the reporting period is not stated.
The 2027 budget does not report on the 1,000km Agricultural Enclave Roads programme.

Two locomotives and 20 wagons were delivered to start freight on Tema-Mpakadan, with signalling upgrades planned for 2027; full commissioning is not reported and the Accra-Kumasi Eastern Line is not mentioned.
Construction of Farmer Service Centres began in 10 districts and 1,840 machines are being procured, against 50 districts and over 4,000 machines.
300mt of maize seed, 300mt of rice seed and 36,506mt of inorganic fertiliser were distributed, far below the 4,388mt, 31,000mt and 272,000mt planned.
No 2026 launch or planting under an Oil Palm Policy is reported; the 2027 budget re-announces 100,000ha of new oil palm as a future New Economy intervention.
The 2027 budget does not report on the seven agro-processing plants.
A transaction adviser was engaged, land secured and feasibility studies are ongoing; no garment factory has yet been established.
The 2027 budget does not report how many MSMEs were helped into AfCFTA markets in 2026.
The 2027 budget does not report on ending double-track SHS.
The 2027 budget does not report on Category B/C school upgrades or E-Block completions.
The 2027 budget does not report on the 200 JHS, 200 primary, 200 KG, teachers' bungalow and toilet programme.
The 2027 budget does not report delivery of mono-desks, buses or pick-ups.
The 2027 budget allocates GH¢292m for free sanitary pads (p.177) but does not report 2026 coverage of all SHSs.
The 2027 budget does not mention the Bunso University of Engineering and Agricultural Sciences.
Work has begun on 160-bed regional hospitals in Oti, Western North and Savannah; the Bole and Shama district hospitals are not mentioned.
The budget refers only to 'the completion of some Agenda 111 hospitals' without a number, so the 10-hospital target cannot be assessed.
The 2027 budget does not report upgrades of seven hospitals for maternal and child health.
MahamaCares-funded services are reported, but no NCD financing policy is mentioned.
The Tamale, Yendi and Damongo water projects are still at the preparatory stage and will start in 2027; commissioning of the Damongo, Bawku and Yendi systems is not reported.
The 2027 budget does not report household or public toilet construction numbers.

Saglemi completion has been rescheduled to 2027 (700 units by March, 806 by December, of 1,506 units); expansion of the Rent-to-Own scheme is not reported (only the separate Rental Assistance Scheme, 917 beneficiaries).
The 2027 budget does not report new cell sites built in 2026.
The 2027 budget does not report Girls-in-ICT training numbers.
The LEAP household ceiling was raised from 350,000 to 400,000 and all 350,000 existing households were reassessed, but actual enrolment of 400,000 households is not stated.
19,760 persons with disabilities benefited from the Disability Common Fund (p.160), but the rise in the DACF share from 3% to 5% is not reported.
Acquisition of four helicopters and a Falcon 6X advanced, with one H175 delivered (p.167); the two Offshore Patrol Vessels are now to be acquired in 2027.
The 2027 budget does not report fire tenders procured in 2026 (it allocates GH¢150m for a Phase 2 retooling in 2027).
2,300 acres (about 930ha) of degraded land were reclaimed by September 2026, with another 370 acres (150ha) under way, against a 10,000ha target.
No new stadium is reported completed; the 2027 budget allocates GH¢600m to begin construction of 10 regional stadia in 2027.
The 2027 budget does not mention the Independent Fiscal Council being constituted.
The Value for Money Office was established after passage of the Value for Money Office Act, 2026 (Act 1172).
NIB, ADB and Consolidated Bank Ghana have been fully recapitalised to meet Bank of Ghana capital requirements; a performance-monitoring framework follows in 2027.
GDP and CPI rebasing were only about 50% and 53% complete at end-September 2026 and are now due in 2027; Tourism Satellite Account surveys were completed, but 'Ghana in Numbers' is not mentioned.
The 2027 budget does not report whether benchmark domestic bond issuance resumed in 2026.
The banking NPL ratio fell to 14.0% in September 2026 from 20.4%, still above the 10% end-2026 target.
The 2027 budget gives no total of jobs created in 2026 to compare with the 800,000 target.
The Registrar of Companies registered 121,960 new entities against 180,000 (p.164), and EOCO recovered GH¢73.9m against about GH¢250m in 2026; both are short of target.
